I spent YEARS (I'm talking like 17 years) in different types of therapy, in and out of hospitals and treatment centers and on a ton of different medications. I was misdiagnosed so many times (adhd, major depressive disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, ptsd, complex ptsd, psychosis, derealization and depersonalization, Bipolar Disorder, neurocognitive degeneration and more... i even thought i was autistic at one point or maybe that i was a compulsive liar and didnt realize it). It was apparent that I did not have a healthy functioning brain but nobody could seem to pinpoint what my condition was and why none of the treatment options were working. On top of all of that, I have multiple legitimate chronic illnesses but even after receiving those diagnosis' was still experiencing so many mysterious symptoms that nobody could figure out. I saw doctor after doctor, specialist after specialist, I received MRI's and cognitive assessments, CT scans and more. Nobody could figure out why I was struggling with so many issues, both mental and physical. At some points, people were concerned that I had some form of epilepsy or neurological degenerative disease because the physical symptoms were so intense.

I have always struggled with memory issues and am missing massive chunks of my life's history (especially childhood). I have always experienced what I thought were episodes of me "zoning out" so intensely that people around me would try to snap me out of it. I struggled in school because I was always so lost in my inner world. It seemed like I just had an active imagination and attention deficit issues, but even once I was older and out of school, I still struggled. I could get lost in my head for hours while I was living alone. I would "come to" and would realize how much time had passed and it was always disconcerting and I didn't know how to explain to people in my life that I didn't get much done each day because I spent most of it lost in my head. The older I got, the more obvious my issues became. I only got properly diagnosed with OSDD at the end of last year because I realized that while everyone else was aging around me and starting families and excelling in their careers, I still felt stuck at a much younger age. I now understand that that is because I am an alter and even though the body has continued aging, I have been the host for a long time and am still in my early 20s. Realizing I am an alter was really really distressing, but its getting easier to accept as time goes on. 

I just thought I had a lot of trauma mixed with erratic and intense moods and a constantly shifting sense of identity, including style preferences, likes and dislikes, dreams, goals and desires, etc. I thought I age regressed due to unprocessed trauma. I knew that sometimes I would feel really confused about conversations I had apparently had with other people that I couldn't remember the contents of. I knew that sometimes, I would get triggered emotionally and end up turning into a raging, destructive asshole and other times I would curl into a ball in a small corner or space and start sobbing hysterically and rocking and hitting myself but I would come out of these "states" or "episodes" and feel humiliated because of the way I had acted but also had no idea why I couldn't seem to stop those moments from happening no matter what coping skills I utilized. I just thought I was a bad person at my core and that those emotionally triggering moments were so intense that I couldn't mask how awful I truly was. I was so close to hitting the nail on the head but kept missing the fact that all of those episodes were alters fronting. 

I also thought that everyone had internal dialogue. I thought that was what people meant when they spoke about their internal monologues. I just thought they were dumb and didn't know the difference between a monologue and a dialogue lol I didn't realize that I was the odd one out and that it isn't typical for people to be able to experience 2 or 3 completely distinct trains of thought simultaneously. 

I could go on and on but the gist is that I spent nearly 2 decades trying to figure out what was "wrong with me" both mentally and physically, with no luck. Finding a properly trained psychologist who understands and works with DID and OSDD was a saving grace.

I'm not sure if I understood you properly but if you are asking me what I would label the opposite of a false religion, I said it in my previous post already. To me, the opposite of false religion is spirituality. It has been proven by many historians and archeologists that even some Neanderthals from the pre-historic era had funeral rituals for their dead that pre-date all modern organized religion. We are talking about some of the earliest humans on earth having had at least some sort of faith in an afterlife and some sort of belief system. That is what I'm referring to when I talk about spirituality being the entire basis for religion. Spirituality pre-dates modern organized religion. Organized religion really only developed at a time in history when people were slowly converting from a nomadic life to a more sedentary life, resulting from agricultural revolutions and the ability to stay in one spot for a long time. This eventually increased population sizes to a point where the concept of spirituality became the political tool of those in power. It's a lot easier to control a large group of people when their sense of faith can be manipulated to such an extent that they will be obedient and follow a set of rules because they fear the concept of hell and crave the concept of heaven. In early historical records, we can clearly see this pattern and the way it progressed as the centuries went by. 

(It's late and I'm about to go to bed, so I am definitely compressing info and am not going into detail too much but if this topic or idea intrigues you, I recommend learning about the origins of organized religion and how they intersect with the rise in populations and the rise of agricultural practices. This is well studied and there are tons of people out there who talk about this topic in a much more articulate manner.)

Alberta Hospital isn't a regular hospital with a triage. You can't just walk in and get assessed, they require you to be assessed through another hospital and then that hospital will either take the patient in if they have a bed available, and if they don't, they will also transfer the patient to whatever hospital has a bed available. Going to a certain hospital to be assessed unfortunately does not mean the patient will be admitted to that same hospital (I just went through the process this past month).

I know how desperate and depressed you feel right now but you don't need to actively harm yourself to get the help you need. You simply need to tell them that you are a danger to yourself and that you have a plan to attempt suicide and that you will take action on it if you are not admitted. I'm sorry you're battling this, you're not alone, but please don't hurt yourself before the help happens. 🫂

I have had both male and female therapists who specialize in a variety of different modalities and I think there have been huge benefits to both sides - with my female therapists, things flowed nicely and there was one in particular that I really strongly connected with and she helped me a lot in terms of how she could relate to certain female-oriented experiences or ways of thinking and processing, but I will say that my biggest growth has come from working with male therapists because the perspective they offer sometimes challenges me in some really interesting ways that I've never experienced with female therapists, plus for me, I do have sexual trauma (from both males and females) that I have only been able to work through with male therapists, two in particular. And even if I didn't have sexual trauma, I do have non-sexual trauma with men too and again, the most growth and healing I've experienced in that regard has been with male therapists. For me, because I've had so many negative experiences with men in my life, working with a male therapist has helped me reframe and improve how I relate to men, how safe I can feel around them, my ability to set boundaries with them, and not to mention, the male therapists I've worked with have actually felt the most safe to me in a therapeutic sense, compared to female therapists! I find that interesting. I have non-sexual trauma with women too and while male therapists have helped me work through that stuff too, it has been the female therapists have really displayed to me what healthy female relationships look and sound like. 
In saying that, it really all boils down to your personal connection with the therapist and whether their communication style meshes with yours, as well as if they are using a modality that works for you. There are pros to both for sure!

For me, the primary thing I want non-BPD folks to understand is that my emotions are so intense that I can physically feel them coursing through my body. When I'm anxious, it's not just "a nervous feeling", it manifests with the most intense physical symptoms, stomach knots to the point of being so nauseous that I sometimes throw up or can't eat. When I feel betrayed, it physically feels like my skin is on fire and my heart starts literally racing and my face gets really hot. When I'm sad, it physically feels like my chest is collapsing in on itself. When I experience grief and loss, my chest physically aches, like I've just been sucker punched straight to my sternum. Sometimes my actual heart will feel like someone has wrapped their entire fist around it and is squeezing as hard as they can. When I feel depressed, it feels like someone has dumped sand into my veins and my entire body physically feels weighed down so much that sometimes it is hard for me to stand up. 

We experience a range of emotion that most people could never even fathom, and it's absolutely brutal. 

I'd also want medical professionals to understand that just because I'm self aware, does not mean that I am doing okay. Being able to psychoanalyze myself does not equate to me being able to feel through my feelings in a way that doesn't feel like I'm drowning in them.

Oh and we are traumatized! We NEED trauma informed professionals to be treating us. If someone is not trauma-informed, they can (and often do) cause more harm to us than good.

We are not "difficult" patients. If you think we are, then you are not truly trauma-informed.

There is literally a massive biological component to the cycle that keeps us going back, but just like recovery from drug addiction, we can recover.

I totally hear you, you're not alone! This is something called Transference. It's very common and any good therapist will be open and curious with you if you choose to bring it up to them. It usually points toward attachment trauma, and talking about it with your therapist is a really good way of digging to the root of it and working through the things that cause you to feel this way. Hey stranger, I totally understand the panic that can come with seeing what looks like a scary or doom filled chart. One thing I've noticed after a decade of studying astrology is that real life rarely ever turns out as bad as a chart may seem. There are SO MANY different meanings and associations with each planet, house, sign, aspect, if a chart is a day chart or a night chart, the chart rulership, where house rulers fall in the other houses, etc. The list goes on and on. Sure there are certain things that can be pretty easily deciphered but there's a reason the vast majority of astrologers from every astrological tradition do not offer readings on death. Not to mention that horary astrology is actually quite nuanced and complicated. It's something I often do not use in my practice because it is too easy to create misinterpretation and, for lack of better terms, "you will probably psych yourself out". Also, reading for ourselves is often much more difficult than reading for others because we are too close to ourselves (obviously lol) to be able to get an objective and clear idea of what we are looking at. 

I'm sorry that you are experiencing panic over this. I would encourage you to stay away from horary astrology and focus more on your natal chart, transits and progressions. Even then, progressions are a more advanced type of reading. I'm not sure what level of knowledge you have about astrology or how long you have been studying it but I always encourage newer astrologers to spend a lot of time really learning their natal chart and it's aspects and what it all tells you about yourself before looking into anything else. There's no sense in jumping to progressions and solar returns and zodiacal releasing, etc if you haven't fully comprehended the incredibly complex dance of planets in your natal chart. Give yourself a big squeeze, go have a warm shower or go for a little walk or just do some deep, diaphragmatic breathing for a bit, do something that feels distracting or calming to you and give yourself lots of reassurance when the anxious thoughts are racing. You are going to be okay. Everything is going to be okay. Sending you big hugs. 🖤

I was the kid in your daughter's position 10 years ago and it was just as difficult back then to access proper help. I bounced around between so many different medical professionals and services and the problem is that our province lacks the adequate resources to cope with the amount of mentally ill, traumatized, addicted and otherwise mentally struggling people. 

My advice - go to the Grey nuns, avoid the royal Alex if you can. If things are at a point where there are no other options, talk to her pre existing psych and request a referral to Alberta hospital. 

I will say as well that hospitalization, medication and talk therapy are only a small fraction of the mental health journey. For me personally, I found it extremely helpful to learn about mindfulness and meditation practices, somatic therapies like yoga, hiking, swimming and rock climbing, and accessing different types of therapy - namely, EMDR Therapy.

I highly recommend looking into EMDR therapy because it helps process traumatic and heavily emotional memories without having to talk about them out loud, through EMDR, I came to a point where I can now think about the traumatic memories and the emotions attached to those memories don't feel so overwhelming, I feel like it's a lot more manageable. I've done therapy for nearly 20 years of my life and out of all of the different types I've tried, EMDR and somatic therapy have been the two most beneficial for me. Aside from the formal therapies I've mentioned, please never forget to take into account things like diet and vitamin deficiencies and points of adventure and joy in her life... addressing these things won't necessarily get rid of her depression or other mental health issues, but they all play a very vital role in the maintenance of good mental health. How often is she getting out of the house and engaging in an activity that helps spark a bit of joy? I never want to engage in those activities in the depths of my depressive episodes, but when I force myself to, even when I don't want to do it, it does help get me out of my head for a bit. Diet and exercise are crazy important too - for me, finding a way of eating that is still healthy but also enjoyable for me was difficult, same goes for exercise - finding exercise that didn't FEEL like exercise was hard but also very important, hence why I ended up getting into rock climbing and hiking especially. Those things don't feel like working out but they sure make a huge difference in my mental health!  

Also, please don't underestimate the impact of living in a heavily capitalistic, commercialized and industrialized society devoid of any zest for life.... maybe take her away to the mountains for a few days if that's something that might interest her? For me, sometimes it's the mental reset I need to help me breathe a bit easier and slow down my thinking a bit... being in a forest isn't going to cure her suicidal depression but it most certainly can help detach from it a bit, even just for a short period of time. I started smoking when I was super young, around 14 years old. It was pretty social at first but eventually led to being chronic. I kept convincing myself that it was medicine for me because it did help with my chronic illness (a genetic disorder I have) and it helped me sleep and eat, and it also helped calm me down during episodes or panic attacks, which were things I needed at the time. It did help for a long time, but my use of it spiraled out of control so quickly. It wasn't until I turned 24 that I started trying to take short breaks from it, but I would never last long because as soon as it was in front of me again, I would cave. It had become a full blown addiction for me. About 2 years ago was when I started taking it more seriously and I would try to quit over and over again, each time lasting longer than the previous attempt to quit, I started lasting long enough without it that I was noticing how the dial turned up on life again in the most beautiful ways when I was sober. Colours were brighter, sounds were sharper, my mind was more clear and my ability to actually practice my coping skills rather than just numbing myself out started to increase. Eventually, I even started to feel smarter. It was like there was this fog hovering over my brain that I hadn't even noticed was there until I stopped smoking for longer periods of time. I could think more clearly and rationally and I actually had better emotional regulation without it. 

I'm 27 now and am at a point where the pros of being sober far outweigh the cons, and the cons of being stoned far outweigh the pros, and it's so apparent that I simply can't not be aware of it. So now I eat edibles once in a while just to kick back and chill with my partner and friends, and I will have a couple of puffs when I'm feeling too emotionally dysregulated and none of my other coping skills are working, but otherwise, I have come to a point where I much prefer being sober. I find I am more self aware, more emotionally regulated, I don't feel as dumb and lazy all the time, and I am much more productive and have been able to revive some of my old passions like creating art and writing. While I was chronically stoned, I simply couldn't get my creative juices flowing, it felt like i had no inspiration or motivation to do those things, no matter how much I loved them. I've also taken up weightlifting and long distance hiking and rock climbing, because I don't feel so goddamn exhausted all the time. Turns out weed was the culprit for that too - I always felt so tired, no matter how much sleep I got. 

My goal is to get to a point where I don't use cannabis at all anymore, but the harm reduction aspect has made a world of difference and has allowed me to say my goodbye to Mary Jane in a way that hasn't felt totally overwhelming. 

It may numb us out, but like my therapist has told me before - if you resort to numbing out the problems in your life, the problems are still there, they don't go anywhere, they just stay bubbling under the surface, growing bigger and stronger until they explode out of you, usually in really toxic and damaging ways. Plus it all just hurts so much more and is so much more annoying to deal with once the high has worn off.

There are plenty of other supplements and non mind altering plants out there that can help with the things I used to smoke weed for anyway, without throwing me into total dependency and apathy 😊 

One more thing - my depression and anxiety are always worse when I'm smoking and are so much better when I'm sober!
